newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parties prepare for battle amid poll fever.
newsitem.headline: French parties prepare for battle amid poll fever.

text.p: Election fever gripped France on Sunday as speculation mounted that conservative President Jacques Chirac would announce a snap general election on Monday to clear the decks in the drive for a single European currency.
Opinion polls showed voters would approve of bringing forward the vote due next March and predicted a close battle.

Amid apparently orchestrated leaks by pro-government politicians, Chirac's office remained tight-lipped except to deny a report in the daily Le Monde that the president was planning a sharp shift towards free-market economic policies.
Political sources said he would go on television on Monday to call a two-round election on May 25-June 1 or June 1-8.

Le Monde said Prime Minister Alain Juppe would set out campaign policies on Tuesday including a new round of austerity -- speeding up tax cuts and limiting the role of the state -- to help France qualify for European monetary union.
"The allegations contained in that article concerning a so-called instruction on a change in economic policy are completely baseless," Chirac's spokeswoman said.
Despite the lack of official confirmation, the centre-right coalition and opposition parties sparred to all intents and purposes as if a short, sharp campaign had started.
"There are factors which can justify an early election," Industry Minister Franck Borotra told Europe 1 radio.

"The government is cleaning up state finances. Can we lose eight months of reforms? We have to maintain and increase the pace of reforms, and we have to adapt the calendar to European and single currency deadlines," he said.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, head of the main opposition party, told TF1 television that a snap election would amount to an admission of defeat for the ruling coalition.
"If the government had any confidence in the success of its policy, it would calmly wait for elections in a year," he said.

In a further cooling towards the single currency, Jospin said that if elected he would introduce no further austerity measures to stop the public deficit overshooting the three percent target needed to join the single currency or Euro.

"If to respect the criteria of three percent, which Germany will probably not respect, if to do that we have to impose, with the jobless rate we have...a new cure of austerity on the country my answer is no. No to the absolute respect of the three percent criterion," he said.
He added he was still in favour of the Euro, an issue which has so far prevented an electoral pact with the Communists.
Outlining his party's programme, Jospin said it would seek to revive growth by boosting purchasing power, and to cut working hours to boost employment.

Veteran deputy Jacques Baumel, a member of Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, said the president was tempted by a snap election "because we need a strong message to the nation and a government reshuffle would not be sufficient.
"We must spare ourselves nine months of campaigning. There are vital economic decisions on Europe due soon and it is important the people be consulted," he told France-2 television.
Fellow RPR deputy Patrick Devedjian said a dissolution was not indispensable but could be useful to the government, even if it risked losing "at least 150 seats".
The centre-right has an overwhelming 478 of the National Assembly's 577 seats following a landslide defeat of a Socialist government in 1993.
The presidency would not be directly affected by the vote. Chirac was elected in 1995 and has another five years to serve. But a left-wing victory could make him a premature lame duck.

A clear majority of voters are dissatisfied with both Chirac and Juppe and 59 percent (against 38 percent) would welcome an early general election, according to an IFOP opinion poll published on Sunday by the weekly Journal du Dimanche.

The poll said 56 percent disapproved of Chirac's performance against 55 percent a month ago, and 31 percent approved against 32 percent in March. Sixty-one percent had a negative opinion of Juppe against 60 percent in March, and only 27 percent had a favourable opinion against 29 percent.
Recent polls have predicted a close battle but differed on whether the centre-right or the left would win.

Chirac is expected to argue that a snap poll is needed to prepare France for a crucial year in European integration. The EU is due to decide early in 1998 which countries meet the criteria to join the single currency due to be launched in 1999.
